title: The Camp Rumour
subtitle: A school vaccination camp meets a video of fainting children
coldOpen: 09:00. A measles camp opens at the quarter’s school.
09:40. A video of fainting children spreads.
Parents are pulling their children out of the queue.

briefing.grievance: Parents want to know if the vaccine is safe and why nobody told them about the camp before a video did. Health workers want the queue back before the vials expire.
knownFacts: The camp is part of a measles catch-up after twelve cases in the quarter.
Two children fainted in the heat before being vaccinated; both are fine.
The vials must be used today once opened.
unverifiedClaims: The video shows children “collapsing after the shot”.
A message says the batch was recalled elsewhere.
briefing.responsibility: You run the health office and the camp. The outbreak is real; so is the fear.
briefing.objective: Answer the video with facts, keep the camp open with consent, and protect the health workers.

rightsMoments.question: A real outbreak meets a false video. Parents are refusing. What may the state do?

options.text: Inform, persuade and make vaccination easy; act on consent, and reserve compulsion for a lawful, proportionate public-health order.
options.feedback: Correct. Bodily autonomy and informed consent are the default; compulsion needs law, necessity and proportion.

options.text: Detain refusing parents until they sign; the outbreak justifies it.
options.feedback: Detention to extract a signature is neither consent nor a lawful health measure.

options.text: Nothing; the state cannot act on health at all.
options.feedback: The state has a duty to protect public health; it must do so through lawful, proportionate means.

rightsMoments.principle: Article 21 covers bodily autonomy and informed consent; public-health powers must be exercised by law and proportionately, persuading first and compelling only where necessary.
rightsMoments.why: A log, a map and a doctor at the gate brought parents back; a locked room would have emptied the quarter.

source.label: Constitution of India, Articles 21 and 22 (India Code)

simple.question: A real outbreak meets a fake video. Parents are refusing. What may the state do?

options.a: Explain, persuade and make the shot easy. Ask for consent.
options.c: Nothing. Health is not the state’s job.

feedback.a: Yes! Consent first. Force only by law, and only if truly needed.
feedback.b: No. Holding people until they sign is not consent.
feedback.c: The state must protect health, but fairly.

simple.principle: Your body is yours. The state explains and persuades first. Force needs a law and a real need.
simple.why: A log, a map and a doctor brought parents back. A locked room would have emptied the quarter.
